Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Overview
Refactoring for Testability and Maintainability
Make design improvements confidently by relying on tests as a safety net and by extracting focused components.
In this lesson

You will learn the Red-Green-Refactor rhythm, detect code smells that block testing, and apply extraction patterns that produce testable units.

Why it matters

Small, test-backed refactors reduce future bug risk, speed feature work, and make code easier for collaborators to reason about.

Explore Key Topics
Refactor safely

Extract components

Design with TDD

Red, Green, Refactor

Extract

screens.title: What is Refactoring in TDD?
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring is a disciplined technique for improving code structure while keeping its observable behavior unchanged. Within TDD it has a specific role: after you make a failing test pass, you enter a refactor phase where you simplify names, remove duplication, and extract smaller pieces. This process improves testability because smaller, well-named units are easier to specify with focused unit tests. For example, a long method that validates input, calls an external A P I, and updates state can be split into a validator, a pure processor function, and a persistence service. Each extracted unit can then be tested with tight unit tests, while the old integration test — a characterization test — ensures the end-to-end behavior remains stable. A common misconception is that refactoring changes performance or requirements; in truth, refactoring improves internal design but must not alter external behavior. Another pitfall is refactoring without passing tests: if tests are already failing you have no safe baseline and should repair tests first. As you practice, prefer many tiny refactors over one large rewrite. A guiding question: does this change make the behavior easier to test and reason about?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Definition
Refactoring
Restructure working code to improve readability, reduce duplication, and increase testability without changing behavior.
Why it matters: Makes units smaller and easier to test in isolation.
Misconception: Refactorings are not feature changes; they are internal improvements.
Safety: Ensure tests pass before and after each change.
Key Takeaway

Small, test-backed refactors are low risk and high reward for maintainable code.

Analogy
Think of refactoring as reorganizing a messy workshop: you keep the tools and parts the same but group them sensibly so future work is faster and errors are less likely.
Example
Split a long method into three collaborators: validator, processor, and persistence service. Test each collaborator independently, and keep an integration test that ensures the original behavior.

screens.title: Red, Green, Refactor — The TDD Rhythm
screens.narratorSegment: The Red-Green-Refactor cycle gives you a repeatable process for changing design while keeping behavior intact. First, write a failing test — this is the Red step and it clarifies the required behavior. Second, implement the minimal code to make the test pass — Green. Keep the implementation intentionally simple so you have a clear baseline. Third, refactor: improve names, reduce duplication, and extract responsibilities, all while running your tests to guard behavior. A concrete example: if your integration test shows the payment processor accepts valid cards and updates balances, start by writing a characterization test that captures that end-to-end behavior. Next, write focused failing tests for a new CardValidator class, implement just enough validation to pass, and wire it back into the processor. Finally, refactor the processor to accept the new validator via dependency injection and simplify its logic. A common mistake is to bundle too many changes into one pass; instead, make one small change per test run. End by asking: which failing test will you write first to drive your next refactor? Red, Green, Refactor — The TDD Rhythm means use small red-green-refactor iterations: narrow the change, implement minimally, and then clean structure with tests confirming behavior.. In practical terms, a reliable cycle for safe design changes.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Code Smells That Harm Testability
screens.narratorSegment: Code smells are surface symptoms that often point to deeper design problems that reduce testability. Common examples include a long method that performs many steps, a large class handling multiple responsibilities, duplicated logic scattered across modules, and feature envy where one object frequently accesses another's internals. Each smell makes focused unit tests harder to write. For example, a method that fetches data, transforms it, and persists results is difficult to test in isolation because a test must set up fetch and persistence. By contrast, separating these steps into three collaborators makes tests simpler and less brittle. A typical misconception is thinking that a single large class is fine if tests exist; in fact, tests may be more complex and brittle if they must exercise many interactions. Use tests as a diagnostic: if you struggle to mock or assert a single behavior, that indicates a smell to address. A practical rule: when one test must prepare five things to run, consider extracting responsibilities until tests need only one clear setup. Code Smells That Harm Testability means if writing a focused test feels complex, the code likely needs extraction or dependency inversion to simplify testing.. In practical terms, recognize symptoms that indicate refactoring is needed.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Code Smells
Typical smells
  • Long method: does many tasks and resists a single unit test.
  • Large class: multiple reasons to change and many dependencies to mock.
  • Duplicate code: scattering logic increases test surface area.
  • Hard-coded dependencies: instantiation inside methods prevents mocking.
Common Pitfall

Ignoring smells because tests exist increases future maintenance cost and test brittleness.

Concrete contrast
Before: PaymentProcessor handles validation, gateway calls, logging, and persistence.
After: Extract CardValidator, GatewayClient, Logger, and UserBalanceService — each tested separately.

screens.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
screens.narratorSegment: The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class or module should have only one reason to change. This matters for testability because classes with a single responsibility expose a focused set of behaviors that unit tests can target directly. Consider a PaymentProcessor that validates, contacts a gateway, logs, and updates balance: it violates SRP and makes tests complex because you must control validation, network, and database behavior in each test. By extracting a CardValidator and UserBalanceService and by making the processor an orchestrator, tests become smaller: validate card behavior can be exercised without touching persistence, and balance updates can be tested without network calls. A common misconception is thinking SRP is about file size; instead, it is about reasons to change. If your tests often fail when unrelated features change, that indicates multiple responsibilities are tangled. The practical rule is to ask: when this class needs to change, is the change for a single cohesive reason? If not, extract the part that would change for that different reason and test it separately. How would you split responsibilities in the last class you touched?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Single Responsibility
SRP in practice
Each class should have a single reason to change, which makes its tests specific and stable.
Example: Extract CardValidator to test validation rules separately from orchestration.
Benefit: Fewer mocks per test and clearer failure signals.
Scenario card
Given a PaymentProcessor that mixes validation and persistence, extract the validation logic and provide a test for the validator alone. Afterward, assert that the PaymentProcessor orchestrates calls to the validator and the balance service rather than containing their logic.

screens.title: Dependency Injection for Testability
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection means giving a component the collaborators it needs instead of having it create them internally. This simple change makes unit tests much easier because a test can inject lightweight test doubles instead of trying to intercept real network or database calls. In the PaymentProcessor example, passing a gateway_service and a logger into the constructor allows tests to provide a mock gateway that returns predictable transaction IDs and a test logger that records messages without writing to production logs. A common misunderstanding is that dependency injection is an advanced framework-level feature. In practice it's often just passing an extra parameter or constructor argument. Use DI when a class depends on external behavior that you will want to control in tests. Also consider factories for complex setup or simple interfaces for gateway clients. After you inject dependencies, keep tests focused: one test per collaborator behavior, and orchestration tests that assert the right interactions using mocks. Ask yourself: which internal instantiations in your code prevent simple test doubles from being used? Dependency Injection for Testability means accept collaborators from outside to allow substitutes during tests and reduce coupling to environment.. In practical terms, pass dependencies so tests can substitute mocks and stubs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Small change: pass gateway_service into the constructor instead of creating it inside the class. Tests can then provide a mock.
Concrete example

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Starter Code
Starter file: payment_processor.py
import logging

class PaymentProcessor:
    def __init__(self, gateway_service, logger=None):
        self.gateway_service = gateway_service # Imagine this is a real external API client
        self.logger = logger or logging.getLogger(__name__)

    def process_payment(self, user_id, amount, card_details):
        self.logger.info(f"Attempting to process payment for user {user_id}, amount {amount}")

        # 1. Validate card details
        if not self._validate_card(card_details):
            self.logger.error("Invalid card details.")
            return {"status": "failed", "message": "Invalid card details"}

        # 2. Authorize with gateway
        try:
            transaction_id = self.gateway_service.authorize(card_details, amount)
            self.logger.info(f"Payment authorized with transaction ID: {transaction_id}")
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error(f"Gateway authorization failed: {e}")
            return {"status": "failed", "message": f"Gateway error: {e}"}

        # 3. Update user balance (simulated)
        if not self._update_user_balance(user_id, amount):
            self.logger.error(f"Failed to update balance for user {user_id}")
            return {"status": "failed", "message": "Failed to update user balance"}

        self.logger.info(f"Payment successful for user {user_id}, transaction {transaction_id}")
        return {"status": "success", "transaction_id": transaction_id}

    def _validate_card(self, card_details):
        # Placeholder for complex validation logic
        return len(card_details.get("card_number", "")) == 16 and \
               len(card_details.get("cvv", "")) == 3 and \
               card_details.get("expiry_year", 0) > 2023

    def _update_user_balance(self, user_id, amount):
        # Placeholder for database interaction
        print(f"Updating balance for user {user_id} by subtracting {amount}")
        return True # Assume success for now

# Dummy Gateway Service for testing
class MockGatewayService:
    def authorize(self, card_details, amount):
        if amount > 1000:
            raise ValueError("Amount too high for mock gateway.")
        return "MOCK_TXN_12345"
Responsibilities to extract
  • Card validation logic — candidate for CardValidator
  • Gateway calls — wrap in GatewayClient interface
  • User balance updates — move into UserBalanceService
  • Logging usage — consider passing a logger or wrapper
Practice prompt: write a characterization test for a successful payment and one for invalid card details before you change anything.

screens.title: Characterization Tests — Start Here
screens.narratorSegment: Begin refactoring by writing characterization tests that assert current behavior for representative scenarios. These tests are not exhaustive unit tests; they record how the system currently behaves so you can detect regressions. For the PaymentProcessor, write tests for at least: successful payment, invalid card, gateway error, and simulated failed balance update. Use the provided MockGatewayService to control network behavior. The characterization test for a successful payment should call process_payment with valid card details and assert a success status and a transaction id structure. For the invalid card, assert the specific failure message returned today. When you have these tests passing against the unrefactored code, they become your safety net. screens.title: Pitfalls and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring without tests or attempting a large rewrite in one go are the two most common and costly mistakes. Tests are your safety net: if they are failing before you start, do not refactor. First fix tests so your baseline is reliable. Make refactors in small, verifiable steps and run the suite after each change. Resist premature optimization as a reason to refactor; focus on readability, maintainability, and testability first, and optimize later where profiling identifies real bottlenecks. Automated IDE refactors like extract method or rename are helpful, but always run tests right away. Another trap is changing internal data structures without confirming external behavior; always run tests before and after such a change. If you need to change widely used internal representations, do it gradually and validate through tests. Final reflective question: if you had to make a large structural change, how would you break it into tiny, test-protected steps? Pitfalls and Safety Notes means run tests before refactoring, change one small thing at a time, and verify with the suite immediately after each step.. In practical terms, avoid big-bang rewrites and refactoring without tests.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Refactoring is the deliberate reshaping of working code so its external behavior stays the same while its structure improves. In a Test-Driven Development workflow this becomes practical and safe: you write a failing test, implement the simplest fix, then refactor with your test suite guarding correctness. In this lesson you will learn why refactoring is not an optional cleanup step but an integral discipline that TDD encourages. We will review common code smells that make testing hard, practical extraction patterns like 'Extract Method' and 'Extract Service', and how dependency injection reduces coupling so unit tests can run in isolation. You will also follow a hands-on scenario: splitting a single 'God Object' payment processor into validator, gateway, and balance services using characterization tests first. That scenario demonstrates the rhythm of Red, Green, Refactor and shows how small, test-driven refactors keep risk low. As you go through the screens, notice how tests act like safety ropes and ask yourself: what small extraction could I do in my next change to make testing easier?

By the end of this chapter you will understand how Test-Driven Development and refactoring support each other, and you will be able to identify when code structure prevents clear tests. You will also recognize common code smells such as long methods, large classes, and duplicated logic that signal the need for refactoring. Importantly, you will learn to apply safe, incremental refactorings using your test suite as a safety net — run tests before you change, make one small change, then run tests again. Finally, you will practice extracting responsibilities into focused components, such as moving validation into a CardValidator or state changes into a UserBalanceService, which makes unit tests simpler and more reliable. Each objective ties to hands-on practice where you write characterization tests, extract single responsibilities, and verify behavior stays identical. Remember: tests don't stop refactoring — they enable it. Consider a concrete case: converting a long function that both fetches and saves data into three focused collaborators makes each collaborator easy to test and the coordinator simple to mock. Which small extraction could improve testability in your current project?

This second objectives slide focuses on practice. First, you will write characterization tests that capture existing behavior before you change code. These tests serve as a guardrail so that any refactor preserves current behavior. Second, you will extract responsibilities incrementally — for example, creating a CardValidator and UserBalanceService — using small, test-first steps. Third, you will refactor code to accept dependencies from outside, enabling straightforward substitution of mocks and stubs in unit tests. Finally, you will run full test suites before and after each refactor and keep changes small to reduce the blast radius of mistakes. Each objective is framed with a small mnemonic or visual trick so you can remember the practice during live development: tests first, extract next, inject dependencies, repeat. A quick mental check: if you cannot write a focused unit test for a method, that method likely needs a single-responsibility extraction.

Refactoring is a disciplined technique for improving code structure while keeping its observable behavior unchanged. Within TDD it has a specific role: after you make a failing test pass, you enter a refactor phase where you simplify names, remove duplication, and extract smaller pieces. This process improves testability because smaller, well-named units are easier to specify with focused unit tests. For example, a long method that validates input, calls an external A P I, and updates state can be split into a validator, a pure processor function, and a persistence service. Each extracted unit can then be tested with tight unit tests, while the old integration test — a characterization test — ensures the end-to-end behavior remains stable. A common misconception is that refactoring changes performance or requirements; in truth, refactoring improves internal design but must not alter external behavior. Another pitfall is refactoring without passing tests: if tests are already failing you have no safe baseline and should repair tests first. As you practice, prefer many tiny refactors over one large rewrite. A guiding question: does this change make the behavior easier to test and reason about?

The Red-Green-Refactor cycle gives you a repeatable process for changing design while keeping behavior intact. First, write a failing test — this is the Red step and it clarifies the required behavior. Second, implement the minimal code to make the test pass — Green. Keep the implementation intentionally simple so you have a clear baseline. Third, refactor: improve names, reduce duplication, and extract responsibilities, all while running your tests to guard behavior. A concrete example: if your integration test shows the payment processor accepts valid cards and updates balances, start by writing a characterization test that captures that end-to-end behavior. Next, write focused failing tests for a new CardValidator class, implement just enough validation to pass, and wire it back into the processor. Finally, refactor the processor to accept the new validator via dependency injection and simplify its logic. A common mistake is to bundle too many changes into one pass; instead, make one small change per test run. End by asking: which failing test will you write first to drive your next refactor? Red, Green, Refactor — The TDD Rhythm means use small red-green-refactor iterations: narrow the change, implement minimally, and then clean structure with tests confirming behavior.. In practical terms, a reliable cycle for safe design changes.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Code smells are surface symptoms that often point to deeper design problems that reduce testability. Common examples include a long method that performs many steps, a large class handling multiple responsibilities, duplicated logic scattered across modules, and feature envy where one object frequently accesses another's internals. Each smell makes focused unit tests harder to write. For example, a method that fetches data, transforms it, and persists results is difficult to test in isolation because a test must set up fetch and persistence. By contrast, separating these steps into three collaborators makes tests simpler and less brittle. A typical misconception is thinking that a single large class is fine if tests exist; in fact, tests may be more complex and brittle if they must exercise many interactions. Use tests as a diagnostic: if you struggle to mock or assert a single behavior, that indicates a smell to address. A practical rule: when one test must prepare five things to run, consider extracting responsibilities until tests need only one clear setup. Code Smells That Harm Testability means if writing a focused test feels complex, the code likely needs extraction or dependency inversion to simplify testing.. In practical terms, recognize symptoms that indicate refactoring is needed.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class or module should have only one reason to change. This matters for testability because classes with a single responsibility expose a focused set of behaviors that unit tests can target directly. Consider a PaymentProcessor that validates, contacts a gateway, logs, and updates balance: it violates SRP and makes tests complex because you must control validation, network, and database behavior in each test. By extracting a CardValidator and UserBalanceService and by making the processor an orchestrator, tests become smaller: validate card behavior can be exercised without touching persistence, and balance updates can be tested without network calls. A common misconception is thinking SRP is about file size; instead, it is about reasons to change. If your tests often fail when unrelated features change, that indicates multiple responsibilities are tangled. The practical rule is to ask: when this class needs to change, is the change for a single cohesive reason? If not, extract the part that would change for that different reason and test it separately. How would you split responsibilities in the last class you touched?

Dependency Injection means giving a component the collaborators it needs instead of having it create them internally. This simple change makes unit tests much easier because a test can inject lightweight test doubles instead of trying to intercept real network or database calls. In the PaymentProcessor example, passing a gateway_service and a logger into the constructor allows tests to provide a mock gateway that returns predictable transaction IDs and a test logger that records messages without writing to production logs. A common misunderstanding is that dependency injection is an advanced framework-level feature. In practice it's often just passing an extra parameter or constructor argument. Use DI when a class depends on external behavior that you will want to control in tests. Also consider factories for complex setup or simple interfaces for gateway clients. After you inject dependencies, keep tests focused: one test per collaborator behavior, and orchestration tests that assert the right interactions using mocks. Ask yourself: which internal instantiations in your code prevent simple test doubles from being used? Dependency Injection for Testability means accept collaborators from outside to allow substitutes during tests and reduce coupling to environment.. In practical terms, pass dependencies so tests can substitute mocks and stubs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's read the starter PaymentProcessor code to identify responsibilities you will extract. The class logs activity, validates card data, authorizes a gateway, and updates user balance — four distinct responsibilities tangled together. Here are three compact concepts to remember as you refactor with tests. First, refactoring means changing internal structure without altering behavior; tests confirm that behavior remains stable. Second, code smells like long methods, large classes, and duplicated logic are signals that extraction and simplification will improve testability. Third, dependency injection makes classes easy to test by letting tests supply mocks and stubs. Keep these ideas in mind when you choose which small change to make next: write a test, make it pass, then refactor.
